title: Can an AI editing assistant follow our brand style without forcing a template?
summary: Keep your brand's editing choices while using an AI assistant for source preparation, clear production rules, and an editable Premiere handoff.
body_markdown:
## What you’ll take away


- Separate repeatable production rules from creative judgments.
- Describe why a reference works instead of asking for a vague style match.
- Choose editable source output when the brand's finishing details matter.


## Decide what should stay consistent


A brand may have fixed identity graphics, caption preferences, naming conventions, and delivery formats. It may also prefer a certain tone: restrained, conversational, energetic, or detailed. Those are different kinds of instruction.


Write down the repeatable rules separately from the intended feeling. For an illustrative customer series, the rules might include a readable name strap and captions with a consistent treatment. The tone might call for direct explanations and room for the customer to finish a thought. A rule can be applied consistently; tone still needs editorial interpretation.


## Explain references in terms of decisions


A reference video is more useful when you say what to borrow. “The opening establishes the customer's problem before showing the product” is a clear observation. “Make it feel like this” leaves the assistant guessing whether you mean pacing, color, music, graphics, or story order.


Use references you are permitted to share. Point to specific moments and their purpose, then distinguish them from elements that should not be copied. The next customer may need a different opening even when the series keeps the same identity and caption style.


## Choose a workflow that preserves finishing control


If the brand relies on detailed timing, custom graphics, or a specific finishing process, prioritize an editable handoff. Wideframe's[Premiere export recipe](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/export-premiere/) supports carrying a sequence or selects into that environment. The editor can then apply the brand's final craft choices to the source-based material.


A template can still be useful for a repeated layout or a predictable deliverable. The buying question is whether the tool lets the team make the changes its work requires. Do not assume that all template workflows are restrictive or that an editable project automatically supplies good taste.


## Give the assistant a concrete first job


In Wideframe, start a chat with the relevant footage or project copy and ask for a bounded task: find the customer answers matching the brief, prepare a clean stringout, or produce captions using the chosen constraints. Include the brand instructions that actually affect that task.


Avoid attaching a long brand book without explaining which parts matter. An assistant preparing soundbites needs story priorities and exclusions more than a complete color palette. An assistant making captions needs text and reading preferences more than a broad mission statement. Relevant instructions are easier to apply than a pile of undifferentiated guidance.


## Save the parts that genuinely recur


Wideframe's[build-a-skill workflow](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/build-a-skill/) provides a route for turning a recurring task into reusable instructions. Use it for a defined production job, not a promise to reproduce an editor's entire aesthetic. The task can ask for changing details such as client, source folder, or delivery format.


Keep reference-based creative choices in the current brief when they vary. A new campaign may need a quieter pace or more technical detail. Updating the brief should not require pretending that the brand has only one valid editing rhythm.


## Let the editor judge the choices that carry meaning


The best take may be technically imperfect but emotionally clear. A pause may matter more than a neat runtime. A product shot may fit the palette while failing to explain the sentence. These are decisions to make in the actual sequence.


Use the prepared output as a starting point and keep the source available. If a choice feels wrong, explain the problem concretely: the customer sounds rushed, the heading overstates the answer, or the B-roll distracts from the important detail. That feedback can improve the next bounded request without reducing style to a mechanical formula.


## Build consistency across a series without flattening it


Keep the shared production conventions and let each story earn its own structure. A customer discussing implementation may need a process explanation; another describing a daily frustration may need a direct opening on the problem. Both can belong to the same brand.


Return to the assistant for the preparation tasks that recur, and retain the editor's ability to make exceptions. The practical benefit is a familiar starting point with editable material, not a collection of videos that all appear to have been poured into one mold.
